content: Computer networking enables communication between devices by establishing standardized methods for data exchange across physical connections. Networks operate through the conceptual OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model's seven layers, though the more practical TCP/IP model with four layers (link, internet, transport, and application) is commonly used in implementation. At the physical level, devices connect through various media including copper wire, fiber optic cables, or wireless radio waves. Data travels in discrete units called packetsâchunks of information with headers containing routing information and payload carrying actual data. Network addressing, primarily through IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, uniquely identifies devices on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (like 192.168.1.1) while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses to accommodate the growing number of connected devices. Routing protocols determine optimal paths for data to travel between networks, with algorithms like OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) calculating efficient routes based on various metrics. Network types include LANs (Local Area Networks) covering small areas like offices or homes, WANs (Wide Area Networks) spanning larger geographical regions, and the Internetâa global network of networks. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) ensures reliable, ordered delivery by establishing connections, tracking packet delivery, and requesting retransmission of lost packets. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) offers faster but unreliable transmission, suitable for applications like video streaming where occasional data loss is acceptable. Network security implements mechanisms like firewalls, encryption, and access controls to protect against unauthorized access and data interception. Modern networking increasingly employs virtualization and software-defined approaches, abstracting network functions from hardware for greater flexibility and management capabilities.

scenario.title: Message Routing System
scenario.content: Students create and manage a virtual school network where messages (representing data packets) travel between classrooms through hallways (communication channels). The simulation allows students to configure network topologies, addressing schemes, and routing protocols to optimize message delivery. The system visualizes packet creation, encapsulation, routing, and decapsulation, showing how data moves through network layers. Students can implement different protocols at various layers, observing how each affects performance, reliability, and security. Interactive tools let students introduce network challenges like congestion, packet loss, or security threats, then develop solutions using standard networking techniques. Challenge scenarios require students to design networks with specific requirements (reliability, bandwidth, security) or troubleshoot problematic configurations, teaching both theoretical understanding and practical networking skills.

hypothesis.description: Students will model computer networks by implementing layered communication protocols. They will analyze how network design affects message delivery performance and reliability, and apply appropriate networking solutions for different communication requirements.
